title: STEP import: a closed shell whose mesh is not closed imports silently (faces dropped or mis-trimmed by truck pass as a model)

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Unsafe or wrong output: gouge, collision, wrong G-code, crash, data loss; blocks a cut

labels.name: area:3d
labels.description: 3D milling and finishing

labels.name: in-review
labels.description: Fix pushed on a branch with an open PR; merges at the next cut

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Found while fixing #1548 (PR to follow).

**What happens.** The STEP importer keeps whatever truck's tessellation returns for a shell. Two things can go wrong inside truck without any error reaching us, and both leave a mesh with holes that imports as a normal model:

- A face whose boundary cannot be placed on its surface gets no polygon (`None`). `to_polygon()` skips it (`truck-meshalgo` `tessellation/mod.rs`, `MeshedShape for CompressedShell<.., Option<PolygonMesh>>`), and `shell_facets` (`crates/app/src/geometry/import/step.rs`) never looks.
- A face whose boundary is placed wrongly is trimmed wrongly and loses triangles.

The file says `CLOSED_SHELL` / `MANIFOLD_SOLID_BREP`, the mesh is open, and nothing is refused or flagged (`coarse_mm` is `None`). The stock simulation and every verdict then judge the program against a model with missing walls. That is the Prime Directive's worst case: a silent wrong answer.

**Evidence** (measured on the #1548 branch base, d569372f, with a debug build):

- A 30 mm cube with all 12 edges rounded R3.125, written by solidcore's step-export: imported with no refusal at **14,993 mm3 of 26,286** (57%), 86 unmatched edges. Every planar face had lost a corner and the cylinders part of their area. (#1548 fixes the two causes found on that file; the importer still has no check that would have caught it.)
- After #1548, variants of `testdata/models/fillet_corner.step` with the corner blend bent (weights `1E300, 1E-300`; a knot at `1.0E300`; a zero-length knot span) import with the blend face dropped: 138 facets, open, no refusal. See `import_step_corner_blend::bent_corner_blends_end_cleanly_and_bounded`, which only asserts "bounded and finite" today.

**Expected.** A shell the file declares closed must mesh closed, or the import is refused by name (which shell, how many unmatched edges, where the first one is), the same way #1536 refuses a face that never converges. A face truck returns no polygon for is refused by name on its own. An `OPEN_SHELL` / surface model is out of scope: it may be open.

**Notes.**
- Welding: adjacent faces evaluate a shared boundary point on their own surfaces, so the copies differ by up to about 1e-7; near a patch pole two copies of the vertex differ by about 4e-9 and leave a sliver facet with two welded corners. The test helper `open_edges` in `crates/app/tests/import_step_corner_blend.rs` welds by neighbourhood at 1e-6 and skips collapsed facets; all existing STEP fixtures (`box`, `bspline_dome`, `Milling-test`, `Milling-test-inch`, `sample_ap214`, `lathe_holder_offset`, `empty_list`, `tool_csys_box_iso13399`) measure 0 unmatched edges with it, so the law should not refuse any of them.
- Observation for triage, not verified as a defect of ours: the files solidcore's `step-export` wrote from a bare `brep_to_model` had every face sense inward, and they import with a negative volume and no message. Whether a STEP solid with inward senses should be refused, flipped or flagged is a separate question.

**Done means:** a STEP whose closed shell meshes open is refused by name inside the normal import time, pinned by a fixture with one face truck cannot place (for example a bent variant of `fillet_corner.step`) and by a test that every existing STEP fixture still imports. Each new refusal has a test that fails when its line is deleted.

Related: #1536, #1545, #1548.

body:
Asked for by the maintainer (2026-11-13, in chat): "make an issue of using cadmpeg as file importer then i suppose.. we could open all common cad parts into camcraft that way."

What is missing: Model > Open reads STEP, STL, OBJ and `.sc`. A part saved in a CAD program's own format must first be exported to STEP by the user.

What cadmpeg is (from its crates.io entry, docs.rs page and `LEGAL.md`, read 2026-11-13; its source and format-support document were not read): a command-line converter and inspector for native CAD files, <https://crates.io/crates/cadmpeg>, Apache-2.0, version 0.6.12, very new (about 575 downloads).
- Reads `.sldprt`, `.f3d`, `.FCStd`, `.ipt`/`.iam`, `.3dm`, `.CATPart`, NX and Creo `.prt`, ACIS `.sat`/`.sab`, IGES, STEP, USD text.
- Writes STEP (AP203/214/242), IGES, USD, its own JSON form, and limited native writers.
- Commands: `convert`, `inspect`, `check`, `diff`, `measure`, `query`, `dump`, `formats`, `dialects`.
- Its docs say it "is not a library"; the per-format codecs are separate optional crates.
- Its legal policy forbids vendor SDKs, decompiled vendor binaries, NDA or leaked material and any circumvention of encryption or DRM; decoders come from files the analyst may hold plus public material, with a provenance declaration per decoder PR. It states it is not legal advice.

Wanted: Model > Open, the viewport drop of issue 1450 and the MCP `import_model` tool accept those formats by converting to STEP and loading the result through the existing STEP importer and the existing undoable import command (no second import path).

Open questions (research first; answers go in comments here, then sub-issues are filed):
1. Route. Recommended: an optional external tool - call `cadmpeg convert` when it is installed, and refuse by name ("install cadmpeg to open .sldprt files") when it is not. No crate is added and none of its code is bundled. The alternative, linking its codec crates, is a new dependency: it needs the maintainer's yes and a `docs/decisions/` entry, and its provenance becomes ours to answer for.
2. Format support. Read cadmpeg's format-support document and try real files (made by us in each program, or files whose terms allow it): which formats convert to a solid our STEP importer loads whole, and which lose faces or come out as surfaces only. Offer only the formats that pass.
3. Clean-room. Confirm on the record that reading a user's part geometry through a third-party tool brings no HSMWorks material into the project (CAM data stored inside a part file is never read), and that cadmpeg's byte-analysis method is not used for our own code.
4. How the tool is found (PATH, a setting), which version is the minimum, and how a missing or too-old tool is reported.
5. Browser build: no external process there; say so in the refusal.

Safety (Prime Directive):
- A conversion that drops geometry must not give a model that looks whole. Run cadmpeg's own `check`, read its exit code and report, and refuse or name what was lost; never machine a silently partial part.
- Units: the converted STEP's units are stated in the import summary; a file with no units asks, never guesses.
- Untrusted input: the external process runs with a time limit and an output-size limit, its temp files go in a fresh directory that is removed afterwards, the file path is passed as an argument (never through a shell string), and a crash, hang or garbage output gives a named error and leaves the project unchanged.
- The converted STEP then passes the STEP importer's own guards (issue 1536 and follow-ups).

Done means (for the research): the five questions answered in comments here, the tried formats listed with their results, and the sub-issues filed (each with one priority, one effort, area, "Done means" and "Part of" this issue); then `needs-research` is dropped and this issue is closed naming them.

title: web/build-app-wasm.sh fails to link on stock macOS: Apple's ar leaves the flecs wasm archive empty

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:build
labels.description: Build, CI, release, tests

labels.name: effort:low
labels.description: Mechanical, one file, no new logic (issue-worker-low)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
Follow-up to #1315 (PR #1485), tested on macOS 27 (Apple silicon) with `/bin/bash` 3.2 and BSD sed at `0b4052bb`.

**What happens:** after #1485, the script gets through the sysroot download, the `shasum` check and the `sed` patching on macOS. The link of `camcraft-cli` then fails with `rust-lld: error: … undefined symbol: ecs_has_id` (and `ecs_modified_id`, `ecs_cpp_set`, …). The `cc` crate archives the flecs C objects with Apple's `/usr/bin/ar` and `ranlib`, which only handle Mach-O. The flecs build warns `ranlib: warning: archive member 'flecs_rust.o' not a mach-o file`, and `libflecs.a` comes out at 96 bytes.

**Confirmed fix:** with `AR_wasm32_unknown_unknown=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar`, the archive is 2.1 MB, the script finishes, and `web/check-app-page.sh target/web` passes. `git status` stays clean.

**Suggested change:** on macOS, when `AR_wasm32_unknown_unknown` isn't set, the script finds `llvm-ar` (on PATH, Homebrew's `$(brew --prefix llvm)/bin`, or rustup's `llvm-tools`) and exports it. With none found, it stops with a message naming what to install (`brew install llvm` or `rustup component add llvm-tools`) instead of failing at the link. "Needs:" in the header gains `llvm-ar` on macOS.

**Done means:** #1315's own definition of done. `web/build-app-wasm.sh` and `web/check-app-page.sh` run unmodified on macOS with `/bin/bash` and BSD sed.

body:
Regression from PR #1546 (#1536, merged 5aab848f): the per-face tessellation evaluation cap `FACE_EVAL_CAP` (25 M, `crates/app/src/geometry/import/step_guard.rs:45`) falsely refuses healthy STEP models.

**Evidence** (M5's review of #1546, pullrequestreview-5898774979, posted after the merge):
- Corpus: 75 STEP files (testdata plus a user's project library). Measured peak evaluations on one face in one pass: 32050.STEP 23.1 M (**92 % of the cap**), socket-head screws 16-19 M, 10208 / 22588B 7.3 M. A healthy face can need far more than the "a few million" the code comment and `docs/decisions/1536-step-tess-guard.md` claim.
- **A false refusal:** `10208.STEP` at the user-settable facet budget of 60 M (`step_budget::CEILING`). On main before #1546 it imports (14,866,333 facets at chord 5e-3, 173 s). After #1546 it is refused as "did not converge" on face #1073, which actually converged at 28.07 M evaluations.
- **Why the whole model fails:** the trip returns `Err(Step)` through `step_refine::refine`, which refuses the whole model. Before, a failed finer pass kept the coarser mesh.

**Expected:**
- A face that converges is never refused at any allowed budget. Give the cap real headroom (e.g. about 10x; about 12-15 s on a broken face in release), or scale it with the facet budget.
- When a finer refinement pass trips the cap, keep the coarser pass's mesh (with a note) instead of refusing the whole model, as before #1546.
- The truly non-converging face (the #1536 case) is still refused by name in bounded time.

**Done means:** 10208.STEP imports at the 60 M budget as before; a pin shows that a face converging past the old cap is not refused; the #1536 synthetic and sc_logo cases still refuse by name within bounded time; and the comment and decision file carry the measured corpus numbers.

Related: #1536, PR #1546, #1545, #1548.

body:
Asked for by the maintainer (2026-11-13, in chat): "in the browser tab add checkbox.. That IF a machine is selected, makes "box" showing the machines work envelope.. if its a cylinder, box, whatever. In the end, the fixture and model "sits" on the floor of the envelope, lathes sits on the end of "cylinder".. work it out."

What is missing: a mounted machine's travel limits are used by the checks, but the viewport never shows them, so the user cannot see whether the part and its fixtures fit the machine.

Wanted:
- A checkbox in the Browser panel ("Show work envelope"), enabled only when the active setup has a machine (its own or the document's). Off by default. It is view state, like the setup eye of issue 1494: not undoable, no command, and it never changes what generates or posts.
- When on, the viewport draws the machine's work envelope as a thin outline with faint faces, from the machine definition already loaded (axis travels; no new figures invented):
  - a milling machine: the box of its X/Y/Z travel;
  - a lathe: a cylinder of its swing and its Z travel, on the spindle axis;
  - a machine with rotary axes: the linear-travel box (the rotary reach is not drawn in the first slice).
- Placement: the envelope is drawn where the machine puts it relative to the setup. Mill: the envelope's floor is the table top, and the fixtures and the model sit on that floor (the fixture stack and table position the setup already knows). Lathe: the chuck face is the end of the cylinder, and the part sits on it, along the spindle axis.
- A machine whose definition lacks the figures needed (no travels, no table position) draws nothing and the checkbox says why in its tooltip; no guessed envelope.

Open points for the worker to settle and record in `docs/decisions/`: where the envelope sits when the setup has no fixture or table position stated (suggested: floor at the lowest point of stock and fixtures, centred in XY, and labelled as "not placed"); whether the envelope is the tool-tip travel or the table-relative volume (state which in the tooltip).

Safety: display only. The envelope must come from the same machine figures the travel and collision checks read, so the picture cannot disagree with a refusal. Nothing here loosens or replaces a check.

Done means: with a mill mounted, ticking the box shows the travel box with the model and fixture standing on its floor; with a lathe, a cylinder with the part on its chuck end; with no machine the checkbox is disabled; a machine without travel figures shows the reason; the structural ui test covers the checkbox states and that toggling it changes no command history and no posted output.

title: Bore op: clear a hole wider than one ring by walking rings (or a spiral) out to the wall, instead of refusing it

labels.name: enhancement
labels.description: New feature or request

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P7
labels.description: Owed polish and small fixes

body:
Found while fixing #1556 (decision in `docs/decisions/1556-bore-core-door.md`).

#1556 made the Bore op refuse, by name, any hole wider than `3 x tool diameter + 2 x stock to leave`: its ride is a centre dive, one radial sweep and one ring on the wall, and past that size the dive's disc and the ring's band no longer meet, leaving a core. Detect holes now leaves such holes out of a Bore op with a note.

Enhancement: let the Bore op clear a wider hole itself - concentric rings stepping out from the dive at a stepover under one tool diameter (or an Archimedean spiral), each level ending on the wall ring - so a user boring a Ø20 hole with a 6 mm tool does not have to switch to a pocket op. Detect holes would then stop filtering (or filter only past a stated limit).

Notes for whoever takes it: the cut-level ladder and the cutter-centre disk certificate in `crates/motion/src/machining2d/bore.rs` already carry several passes per level; the links between rings must certify inside that disk. The floor-coverage law test in `crates/motion/src/machining2d/bore_core_tests.rs` (`every_bore_the_ride_takes_clears_its_whole_floor`) should be extended to the wider holes. Engagement of a full-width ring per level is the machining question (stepover choice, maybe a helix entry instead of the centre plunge).

Done means: a Bore op on a hole wider than 3 tool diameters clears its whole floor (pinned by the coverage law over a range of ratios), verify passes it, and the 3d refusal is lifted or moved to the new limit.

body:
Found while fixing #1556.

What happens: #1556's Bore op cut one centre slot and one ring in a Ø74.3 through bore with a 4 mm end mill and left a Ø66 mm disc with nothing joining it to the part. `generate` said ok and `verify` said `ok: true` with no finding - neither the program gate nor the stock simulation asks whether the remaining stock is still one connected piece. #1556 closes the Bore case at its source (the kernel refuses a bore its ride cannot clear, and Detect holes leaves such a hole out of a Bore op, by name), but any other path that cuts a closed loop through the part - an inside 2D Contour through a hole, a Slot ring, a hand-edited hole list on another kind - can free a slug the same way with no word from verify.

Freeing a slug is sometimes intended (an inside profile drops its slug by design, held by tabs or a fixture), so this needs design, not just a check: when is a freed piece a finding, a warning, or expected (tabs, a vacuum table, a known slug op)?

Evidence: with the #1556 kernel door disabled, `crates/app/tests/bore_core.rs::a_bore_op_handed_the_wide_bore_by_hand_refuses_at_generate` generates `ok` for the wide bore - nothing downstream objects.

Done means: a design note answers when a freed piece is reported (and how: a stock-sim connectivity read of the remaining material, or a per-op closed-loop-through check), and the chosen law flags the #1556 shape (a free core in a through bore) on verify, pinned by a test.

title: Setups page: "Pick for WCS" takes no viewport pick - clicks still select the whole model

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: P1
labels.description: Unsafe or wrong output: gouge, collision, wrong G-code, crash, data loss; blocks a cut

labels.name: area:ui
labels.description: User interface and picking

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

body:
Reported by the maintainer (2026-11-13, in chat, on a v0.19.0 build): "this section under Setup<n> is to set WCS - but it cannot really select any edges, points or gizmo axises.. so not sure what its supposed todo?" Priority P1 is the maintainer's ("Make P1 issue for it").

What happens: on the Setups page, the row "Set WCS from features - each pick sets a role" is armed with "Pick for WCS". The status line says to pick faces, edges, corners or walls, but a click in the viewport selects the whole model as usual. Nothing is highlighted on hover, no "Picked: ..." line appears, and Apply never becomes available.

What should happen (issue 701, the row's own hover text): while the row collects, a click on a face, an edge, a corner or a curved wall is taken as the pick for the role in the box (Origin, X, Y, Z), and the hover highlights what the click would take.

Cause, from the code:
- `crates/ui/src/interact.rs` (about lines 104-108) sends a viewport click to `feature_click::click` only when `state.geo_pick` is Face, Edge or Vertex. In `GeoPick::Model`, the default (`state.rs`), the click goes to `pick_model`. The hover has the same gate (about line 185).
- `crates/ui/src/wcs_pick.rs` `arm` leaves `geo_pick` as it is, on purpose ("the toolbar's pick mode is the user's own"). Every other pick draft switches it when armed: `plane_pick` (Face), `points_pick` (Vertex), `axis_pick` (`mode_of(by)`), `locate_pick` (Face), the boundary pick (Model to Edge).
- The only control that changes the mode is "Click selects:" on an operation's Geometry page (`egui_app/geo_page.rs`), which is not shown on the Setups page. So with no operation open the mode is Model and the role draft can never receive a pick. `feature_click::ask` and `click` already handle the armed row correctly (faces, edges and points together); they are just never reached.
- Why the tests did not catch it: `egui_app/wcs_pick_tests.rs` sets `geo_pick = GeoPick::Vertex` by hand or calls `wcs_pick::take` directly. No test arms the row from the default mode and clicks through `interact`.

Not a defect: the gizmo axes are not a pick target of this row by design. If picking a gizmo axis as a role is wanted, that is a separate enhancement.

Suggested fix: while `wcs_pick::collecting(state)`, route viewport clicks and hover to `feature_click` whatever `geo_pick` is (as `wcs_ui.pick_circle` already does for the hover), or have `arm` leave Model mode and restore the previous mode on disarm, pause and Apply. Check the same gate for any other draft that relies on the mode it sets being left alone.

Done means: from a fresh project (pick mode Model, no operation open), arming "Pick for WCS" and clicking a face, an edge and a corner in the viewport records each as "Picked: ..." with its role, the hover highlights the feature under the cursor, and Apply places the WCS; pinned by a ui test that arms the row from the default mode and drives the click through `interact` (not `wcs_pick::take`); disarming gives the previous click behaviour back.

title: 2D ops cannot start below the material top: the entry rapids into uncut stock, so the air pass at Top cannot be avoided

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:2d
labels.description: 2D milling

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:high
labels.description: Several crates, new behaviour with tests; safety floor (issue-worker-high)

labels.name: P7
labels.description: Owed polish and small fixes

body:
Found while programming a simple 2.5D end-cap plate (user's project) with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (macOS arm64), driven headlessly over MCP. Re-checked on upstream main **d00243a5**: **still reproduces, identical output**.

## What happens

Every 2D depth ladder cuts its first level at `top_z` (#514, kept by the maintainer on 2026-11-11). When Top is the faced material top, that level is a full pass in air. The obvious way to avoid it, setting Top to the first real cut, is **refused**: the entry rapids straight down to Top + the plunge height, which is inside the uncut stock above Top, and verify convicts it:

`rapid move 1 travels below the clearance plane inside stock`

So the air pass cannot be avoided. In the user's project the bore adaptive (2D Adaptive, three 0.25 in levels) keeps an air level at the faced top: **about 5.6 of its 16.9 min**.

Repro (main and v0.19.0 alike), a plate in stock 0.5 mm taller, faced to the part top first, `stepdown: 4`, bottom at the part bottom:

| op | `top_z` | levels (z) | first moves | verify |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2D Adaptive (bore) | TOS -0.5 (faced top) | 10 (air), 6, 2, 0 | rapid to z 12, feed down | ok |
| 2D Adaptive (bore) | TOS -4.5 | 6, 2, 0 | **rapid to z 8** (stock is at z 10) | `rapid move 1 travels below the clearance plane inside stock` |
| 2D Contour inside (bore) | TOS -0.5 | 10 (air), 6, 2, 0 | rapid to z 12, plunge | ok |
| 2D Contour inside (bore) | TOS -4.5 | 6, 2, 0 | **rapid to z 8** | same message, moves 1 and 5 |

The rapid law is right to convict a rapid into stock; the generator is what puts it there.

## Minimal repro (MCP)

`plate_bore.stl`: a 100 x 60 x 10 mm plate, centred, z 0..10, with a centred Ø40 through bore.

```
import_model   {"path": "plate_bore.stl", "name": "plate"}
add_setup      {"name": "Setup 1"}
set_stock      {"box": {"dx": 110, "dy": 70, "dz": 10.5}}
set_wcs        {"stock_point": {"x": "center", "y": "center", "z": "max"}}
add_tool       {"catalog": "EM-0600-4FL", "name": "EM6"}
add_operation  {"kind": "Face", "tool": "EM6", "name": "face", "params": {"cut_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -0.5}}}
add_operation  {"kind": "2D Adaptive", "tool": "EM6", "name": "op", "source": "plate",
                "params": {"top_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -4.5},
                           "bottom_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -10.5}, "stepdown": 4}}
set_operation_geometry {"operation": "op", "picks": [the bore's top chain]}
generate {} ; verify {}  -> "rapid move 1 travels below the clearance plane inside stock"
```

## Expected

An op whose Top is below the material standing over it enters safely: it rapids to the plunge height above the **material actually there** (the prior stock, or the stock top), then feeds (helix, ramp or plunge) down to its first level. Then a user can set Top to the first real cut and skip the air pass, without reopening the #514 ladder decision.

## Done means

## What happens

One Ø6 mm through hole (10 mm deep plate, 11 mm cut) with a Circular op and a 4 mm end mill came out as **74,131 moves** (53 rapids, 74,078 feeds, median feed length **0.0061 mm**, no arcs). Posted, that is about 74,000 G1 blocks for one small hole: a huge file, and at 500 mm/min each block lasts under 1 ms, far past what most controls can process, so the machine starves and stutters. The user dropped Circular and used the Bore op (arcs) instead.

Every parameter set tried is in the tens of thousands:

| Circular params (others as below) | moves | median segment |
|---|---|---|
| as below (helix entry R1, stepover 0.5) | 74,131 | 0.0061 mm |
| `entry: plunge` | 13,416 | 0.0123 mm |
| `helix_radius: 0.5` | 13,446 | 0.0123 mm (+ warnings `feed moves 2 and 6737 cross in XY at shared depth`) |
| `stepover: 1.0` or `2.0` | 26,937 | 0.0123 mm |
| `radius: 4.0` | 26,858 | 0.0184 mm |
| `radius: 6.0` | 53,690 | 0.0307 mm |
| `stepdown: 2.0` | 67,989 | 0.0061 mm |

**Cause (read, not fixed).** `ring_loop` in `crates/motion/src/machining2d/circular.rs` writes every ring as a closed polygon of **512 chords** whatever its radius, and the op emits no arcs. A ring at R1 (6 mm hole, 4 mm tool) is 512 chords of 0.012 mm each, at every level. The helix entry ("stands down to a ramp along the first cut") then ramps along that polygon, splitting it further, which is where the 74k comes from. The Bore op on the same hole emits three arcs per ring.

## Minimal repro (MCP)

```
import_model   {"path": "End Caps-End capSupport Plate.step", "name": "part"}
move_model     {"name": "part", "position": [0, 37.9, 4.826]}
add_setup      {"name": "Setup 1"}
set_stock      {"box": {"dx": 110, "dy": 185, "dz": 15.33}}
set_wcs        {"stock_point": {"x": "center", "y": "center", "z": "max"}}
add_tool       {"catalog": "EM-0400-2FL", "name": "EM4"}
add_operation  {"kind": "Circular", "tool": "EM4", "name": "c", "source": "part",
                "params": {"center": [-35.0, 2.9], "radius": 3.0, "stepover": 0.5,
                           "top_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -0.508},
                           "bottom_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -11.524},
                           "stepdown": 1.0, "feed": 500, "plunge_feed": 250, "climb": true,
                           "entry": "helix", "helix_radius": 1.0}}
generate {}   -> 74,131 moves
```

(The project used inch units; these are the same values in mm. Any model and any small circle show it; the hole position is one of the plate's Ø6 holes.)

## Expected

A Circular ring posts as true arcs (G2/G3, a few per ring, as Bore does), and the helix or ramp entry as a helical arc or a few segments; a hole like this is a few hundred blocks at most. Where chords are needed, their count comes from a chord tolerance, not a fixed 512.

## Done means

- The repro above generates under ~500 moves with the rings as arcs; the move count is pinned by a test (with a ceiling per ring and level).
- Path and verify results otherwise unchanged (same radii, depths and direction); CL/NC goldens for Circular regenerated in one commit.

body:
Found while programming a simple 2.5D end-cap plate (user's project) with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (macOS arm64), driven headlessly over MCP, Tormach PathPilot post. Re-checked on upstream main **d00243a5**: **still reproduces, identical directions**.

## What happens

With `climb: true` (the default, shown in the GUI as "Climb milling"), **2D Contour runs conventional**: with the spindle on M3 the outside profile runs **CCW** around the part and an inside (bore) profile runs **CW**. With `climb: false` it runs the other way, which is the real climb. Every 2D contour posted with the default flag is conventional-milled, silently. In the user's project the three contours had to be set to `climb: false` to get climb.

The **2D Pocket**'s wall pass shares the inversion. Other ops are right:

| Op (`climb: true`, M3) | Measured travel at the floor | Correct for climb? |
|---|---|---|
| 2D Contour, outside | CCW (G3 corners) | **no** (conventional) |
| 2D Contour, inside (bore) | CW | **no** (conventional) |
| 2D Pocket, bore wall pass | CW | **no** (conventional) |
| 2D Adaptive, in the bore | CCW (G3) | yes |
| Bore | CCW (G3) | yes |
| Circular | CCW | yes |

Posted output (main, outside contour, `climb: true`; the part spans X ±50, Y ±30):

```
S9500 M3
...
G01 X50.346 Y-32.98 Z-2 F1200
G03 X53 Y-30 Z-2 I-0.346 J2.98 F1200
G01 X53 Y30 Z-2 F1200
G03 X50 Y33 Z-2 I-3 J0 F1200
G01 X-50 Y33 Z-2 F1200
```

That is the tool going up the +X side and across the top to -X: CCW around the part.

**The convention.** With M3 (clockwise spindle seen from above), climb milling keeps the material on the **right** of the tool's travel (the G41 side): an outside profile runs **clockwise** around the part, an inside profile (a hole or pocket wall) runs **counter-clockwise**. Conventional is the reverse. With M4 both reverse.

**Cause (read, not fixed).** `crates/motion/src/machining2d/contour.rs` (around line 207) says "Canonical orientation is material-on-the-left travel; conventional climbing reverses it", and keeps that order when `p.climb != inside`. Material on the left of the travel with M3 is conventional, so the rule is inverted. The unit test `contour_inside_shrinks_and_flips_travel` in `machining2d/tests.rs` pins the same reading ("climb under Inside travels the loop reversed, so material stays on the left"). The GUI label maps 1:1 to the parameter, so the parameter, not the label, is what is wrong. The pocket's wall pass needs the same check (`pocket.rs` / `pocket_hsm.rs` `plan_passes`); also worth checking 2D Chamfer, Slot, Trace and the contour lead/arc side (`arc_leads.rs` `air_side`), which follow the same flag.

## Minimal repro (MCP)

`plate_bore.stl`: a 100 x 60 x 10 mm plate, centred in XY, z 0..10, with a centred Ø40 through bore.

```
import_model   {"path": "plate_bore.stl", "name": "plate"}
add_setup      {"name": "Setup 1"}
set_stock      {"box": {"dx": 120, "dy": 80, "dz": 12}}
set_wcs        {"stock_point": {"x": "center", "y": "center", "z": "max"}}
add_tool       {"catalog": "EM-0600-4FL", "name": "EM6"}
add_operation  {"kind": "2D Contour", "tool": "EM6", "name": "outside", "source": "plate",
                "params": {"top_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -2},
                           "bottom_z": {"reference": "top_of_stock", "offset": -11},
                           "stepdown": 20, "climb": true, "entry": "plunge"}}
set_operation_geometry {"operation": "outside", "picks": [the 4 top outer edges' chains]}
edit_operation {"name": "outside", "params": {"side": "outside"}}
(same again, "inside", picking the bore's top chain, side "inside")
generate {} ; post {"output": "out.nc"}
```

Result: outside CCW, inside CW (signed area of the floor-level feed moves +7276 / -915 mm²). With `climb: false`: outside CW, inside CCW.

## Expected

`climb: true` with M3: outside profiles CW, inside profiles CCW, on every 2D op that takes the flag (and both reversed under M4), matching Adaptive, Bore and Circular today.

## Done means

- 2D Contour (outside, inside, open chains) and the 2D Pocket wall pass run climb as defined above when `climb: true`, conventional when false; pinned by a direction test per op that checks the signed travel at a level against the spindle direction.
- Every other op with a `climb` flag (Chamfer, Slot, Trace, Face rows, leads) checked against the same rule and pinned.
- The test that pins "material on the left" is corrected, not deleted; affected CL/NC goldens are regenerated in one commit.
- The release notes say that contour and pocket direction changed: a project that set `climb: false` as a workaround will now post conventional.

1. Reproduce with 60 x 60 stock and dump the posted path around one corner.
2. Compute the swept tool disc at the stock corner analytically.
3. Compare with the carried body's columns there, and with the in-setup stock sim (not carried).

If the path covers the corner but the carried body keeps it, it's a carry or sim bug: in Setup 2 it can make a fixture or vise falsely collide, or report false rest. If the path really leaves it, it's a contour corner-motion issue.

**Done means:** the probe result is posted here. If a bug, a pin with the 60 x 60 case shows no full-height corner material after the contour, sim-verified, plus the fix.

body:
Found while triaging issue 1510 (maintainer asked for a check against published references, 2026-11-13).

What we do today: a milling setup always cuts along the machine's Z as the model lies. The part is turned for a setup with Part alignment (issue 326). A WCS tilted off Z is refused at generation by name (PR 1518).

What the published documentation of the product we reimplement describes (behaviour only, read through a search summary, not verified page by page):
- The setup's WCS orientation sets the default tool direction: pointing the WCS Z out of another face makes that setup's 3-axis toolpaths cut from that direction; the model is not turned. The operator flips the part on the machine to match.
  - https://help.autodesk.com/cloudhelp/ENU/Fusion-CAM/files/MFG-TOOL-ORIENTATION-OVERVIEW.htm
  - https://www.autodesk.com/products/fusion-360/blog/fusion-360-wcs-tool-orientation/
- G54-G59 are translations on the machine (LinuxCNC also allows a rotation about Z); they do not re-aim the spindle: https://linuxcnc.org/docs/html/gcode/coordinates.html

So the reporter of 1510 used the workflow that documentation teaches. The maintainer's stated view (2026-11-13, in chat) is the opposite design: "You should orient the part to Z using Setup.. Not let the WCS orient the part to Z..". Both give the same posted program for a flipped part; they differ in which control the user turns.

To decide (maintainer):
1. Keep Part alignment as the only way to turn a part (today). Then the WCS pane should not offer a tilt for a milling setup, or should offer "turn the part with Part alignment" at that moment, so a user coming from the reference product is led there before Generate refuses.
2. Or let a tilted setup WCS define the tool direction (generate in the WCS frame; `docs/decisions/1510-tilted-wcs.md` rated that effort:max: every generator, stock, heights, simulation and the post's rotated-offset refusal are involved).

Safety: whichever is chosen, a tilted WCS never generates a path in a frame other than the one shown; the refusal of PR 1518 stays until option 2 is complete.

Done means: the maintainer's choice is recorded here; for option 1, the WCS pane change with its structural test; for option 2, sub-issues filed and this one closed as the umbrella.

Found while programming a small two-sided part with HAT-style stock and soft jaws (user's project), with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (`camcraft-cli 0.19.0`, macOS arm64).

## What happens

Importing `sc_logo.step` **never finishes**. The STEP was exported by SolidCraft 0.41.0, and its bounding box and volume match the design. Under CamCraft v0.19.0 the import:

- ran for **over 19 CPU-minutes** in the user's session without finishing;
- ran the same way with `facet_budget: 200000`;
- **re-run for this issue:** `cam.import("sc_logo.step", "sc_logo")` through `camcraft-cli script`, killed after **10 min 13 s wall (10 min 10 s CPU, 322 MB resident)** with no output and no error (see below).

Nothing in the import is bounded in time. The facet budget does not stop it, because no facet is ever produced. A hang on user input breaks the Prime Directive: the import must finish or refuse by name.

## The model

A **30 mm cube made of two L-shaped halves**:
- the top half is missing the +X+Y quadrant and the bottom half the -X-Y quadrant, which makes two 15 mm-deep quadrant steps;
- **every edge is filleted R3.125 mm**, convex and concave.

STEP content:
- 1 closed shell, 62 faces, 126 edges, 66 vertices;
- the faces are 12 planes, 30 cylinders, 14 spheres and **20 `B_SPLINE_SURFACE_WITH_KNOTS`**, the blends where three fillets meet;
- 106 `B_SPLINE_CURVE_WITH_KNOTS` edges, AP242, 198 KB.

SolidCraft reports the volume as 19549.7 mm3 and the bbox as +/-15 mm.

## Where it spins

`sample` of the process after 4 min (one core busy, all other rayon workers idle). The busy thread is:

```

  camcraft_app::geometry::import::load_model_graded_within
   camcraft_app::geometry::import::step::parse_with_chord_budget
    camcraft_app::geometry::import::step_refine::refine<..., step::shell_facets>
     camcraft_app::geometry::import::step::shell_facets
      truck_meshalgo::tessellation::triangulation::cshell_tessellation<..., by_search_nearest_parameter>
       (rayon par_iter over CompressedFace)
        truck_geotrait::algo::surface::sub_parameter_division<NurbsSurface<Vector4>>
         truck_geometry::nurbs::knot_vec::KnotVec::try_bspline_basis_functions   <- top of stack, most samples
```

So one face's tessellation, very likely one of the 20 NURBS corner blends, never converges in truck's `sub_parameter_division`. The `within` / chord-budget wrapper cannot interrupt it, because the loop is inside truck.

A second sample at 7.7 min shows the same frames. The resident memory grew from 175 MB (at 4 min) to 322 MB (at 7.7 min), so the subdivision keeps refining rather than spinning in place.

// imp.js
cam.import("sc_logo.step", "sc_logo");

title: Posting: one program per setup, or an optional stop between setups

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:post
labels.description: Post processors and G-code

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
Found while programming a small two-sided part with HAT-style stock and soft jaws (user's project), with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (macOS arm64), driven headlessly over MCP, Tormach PathPilot post.

## What happens

A document with two setups (Setup 1 at G54, Setup 2 at G55, with the part flipped between them) posts as **one program**. Setup 2's first operation follows Setup 1's last move with **no program stop** (`M0`/`M1`) and no message to the operator. From the posted file:

```
G1 X1.3127 Y-1.0908 Z-0.2962 F30
G0 X1.3127 Y-1.0908 Z0.9843
M9
M5
(SETUP: Setup 2)
(OPERATION: S2 Face hat off rough - FACE - G55)
G17 G90 G55 G40 G49 G80
...
T31 M6
G43 H31
S9500 M3
M8
```

On cycle start, the machine finishes Setup 1 and **starts cutting Setup 2's path at once**, before anyone has flipped or re-clamped the part. Setup 2's program is then running on a part still clamped for Setup 1. It cuts air at best; at worst it cuts the wrong side of the part, the vise or the parallels at full feed.

To get one program per setup, the user had to delete the other setup's ops from a scratch copy and post again, or cut the file apart by hand.

A per-operation "after" action already exists (`AfterOperation`: optional stop / program stop / go home, #110), and a program-stop entry can be put after an op in the GUI. **Nothing puts one at a setup boundary by default**, and I found no MCP tool that adds a stop entry.

## Expected

The user chooses, per document (and in the post dialog / MCP `post`), between:

1. **one file per setup** (for example `name_setup1.nc`, `name_setup2.nc`, each with its own header, tool list, work offset and `M30`); or
2. **one file with a stop between setups**: an `M0` (or `M1` if the user prefers) after the last op of each setup, with a comment naming the next setup and what to do (`(SETUP 2: FLIP PART, CLAMP ..., G55)`).

**Safety:** the default for a multi-setup document posted as one file should be the `M0` stop, not "run straight on". A program that moves from one setup to the next with no pause is a crash waiting for an operator who expects it to stop. The current default may deserve a higher priority than this issue carries.

**Done means:** posting a two-setup document either writes one file per setup, or writes one file with an `M0` and a setup-change comment between the setups, as chosen. With no choice made, the default never runs from one setup into the next without a stop. The MCP `post` tool takes the choice. A pinning post test covers both modes on at least the Fanuc and Tormach dialects.

Related: #110 (per-operation after-action), #388 (one file per post when setups use different machines), #258 (post dialog options).

body:
Found while programming a small two-sided part with HAT-style stock and soft jaws (user's project), with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (macOS arm64), driven headlessly over MCP.

## What happens

The part is a 30 mm cube made of two L-shaped halves with 15 mm quadrant steps. Every edge, convex and concave, has an R3.125 mm fillet. The only cutter is a 1/4 in (6.35 mm) 3-flute **flat** end mill.

- **3D Finish takes only a ball nose** (`list_operation_types`: `"tool_kinds": ["BallNose"]`). With the flat end mill, the op is refused:
  `No ball-nose in Setup 2's tools - a 3D Finish operation cuts with one; add it ... 'BN-0600' (6 mm ball-nose)`
- There is no **z-level (waterline) finish** with a flat or bull-nose tool. That is the usual way to finish steep walls and convex fillets with the tool already in the spindle.
- The workaround was a **3D Pocket** with 0.15 mm (0.006 in) stepdowns used as "terraces" over the top fillets. That is a roughing strategy, so it leaves the 0.15 mm stair-steps the user has to accept. It also hit `feed moves ... cross in XY at shared depth` on the notch path.

## Expected

A finishing strategy that works with flat and bull-nose cutters:

- **z-level / waterline contours** on the model at a set stepdown (or scallop height), at least for steep regions;
- the tool's real shape (flat bottom, corner radius) used for the gouge offset;
- the shallow areas left to a later pass or flagged as rest.

A flat tool still cannot form a concave fillet smaller than its corner radius, and the rest check should say so. It can follow convex fillets and walls.

**Done means:** 3D Finish (or a new 3D Contour kind) accepts flat and bull-nose tools with a z-level pattern. On a filleted block with a flat end mill it generates gouge-free waterline passes at the set stepdown, and verify reports the concave-fillet rest. A pinning test covers the flat and bull-nose cases.

Related: #763 (3D work in an aligned setup, needed for the same part's bottom side).

body:
Found while programming a small two-sided part with HAT-style stock and soft jaws (user's project), with the CamCraft **v0.19.0** release CLI (macOS arm64), driven headlessly over MCP.

## What happens

In a second setup that takes "what Setup 1 leaves behind" as its stock (part flipped, part alignment), the carried-workholding gate judges each fixture by its **world bounding box**, not its shape. Any fixture whose box encloses the carried part is refused, even when the steel only touches the part's sides.

Cause (v0.19.0): `crates/app/src/fixture_carried.rs::carried_fixture_problems` reads `model::entity_world_aabb(world, &fe)` and passes that box to `penetration()`. Every carried column whose centre lies inside the box's XY footprint and whose material overlaps its Z span counts as a hit.

Refusals seen:

1. **The built-in vise** (`add_builtin_vise`, 5 in, jaws closed on a 50 mm part): its box spans the opening between the jaws, so the part it clamps "stands inside" it.
   `setup 'Setup 2': fixture 'Vise 5 in (2)' stands inside the stock carried from setup 'Setup 1' (4.48 mm deep) - the part that setup leaves cannot be held as modelled; move the fixture or re-check the hold`
2. **A pair of 5.2 x 2 x 1 in aluminum soft jaws with a nest pocket**, imported as one STEP fixture, with the part seated in the nest:
   `fixture 'Soft jaws (nest)' stands inside the stock carried from setup 'Setup 1' (11.43 mm deep) - the part that setup leaves cannot be held as modelled`
   The nest is inside the jaws' box, so the part is "inside the fixture" by definition.
3. The same jaws modelled as 9 plain blocks cut around the nest: the jaw "island" blocks are still refused at **9.93 and 11.28 mm** deep. Those island blocks lie inside the nest's L-shaped notch, below the part's notch floor (3.57 mm clearance as designed). Part of this may be that the Setup 1 3D ops were held, so the carried body there is not fully cut. The box-based judging is the same either way.

The workaround in the user's h5 project: model the vise jaws as two separate blocks instead of the built-in vise.

## Reproduction (headless, `camcraft-cli mcp`)

- The h5 plate: a 50 x 50 x 6 mm plate with 5 mm grooves.
- Setup 1 (top side) machines it from 55 x 55 x 11.3 mm stock in a vise.
- Setup 2 flips it about X (part alignment), uses "what Setup 1 leaves behind", and holds it in two block jaws plus parallels. That verifies and posts clean.
- Then, in Setup 2, place the built-in vise where the block jaws are:

```
open_project {path: h5.camproj}
add_builtin_vise {size: "5 in", setup: "Setup 2", position: [0, 25, -28.798], opening: 50}
verify
post {output: o.nc}
```

-> `verify.gate.problems` and the post refusal: `setup 'Setup 2': fixture 'Vise 5 in (2)' stands inside the stock carried from setup 'Setup 1' (4.48 mm deep) ...`

The vise's jaw faces are at Y +/-25, exactly the part's 50 mm sides. The steel only touches the part; the box reaches across it.

## Expected

The carried-stock fixture check judges the fixture's **real solid**: its mesh, or each body of a multi-body fixture, such as each jaw of a vise or each jaw of a soft-jaw pair. A part seated in a nest pocket, or clamped between jaws, passes. Steel truly inside the carried material is still refused by name.

**Done means:** a built-in vise clamping a carried part on its sides, and an imported soft-jaw fixture with a nest the carried part sits in, both pass the carried-workholding gate. A fixture that really overlaps the carried material (a jaw block moved into the part) is still refused with its depth. Pinning tests cover all three.

Not checked here: whether the in-setup fixture collision check (toolpath vs fixture) has the same box-only limit. It passed for the nest program in a single setup.

Related: #321 (the carried-workholding clause), #637 (carried stock on the field engine), #1511 (soft-jaw presets with a nest).

## What happens

`Top of Model` and `Bottom of Model` resolve to the bounds of **every model in the document, fixtures included**. With a vise placed, a cut referenced to `Bottom of Model` runs down to the **bottom of the vise body**, and `Top of Model` can resolve to the **jaw tops**.

Every 2D/3D milling kind defaults to these references: 2D Contour, 2D Pocket, Slot, Trace, 2D Adaptive, 2D Offset, Engrave, Circular, 3D Pocket, 3D Finish, Deburr and Trochoidal slot (`bottom_z = bottom_of_model`, `top_z = top_of_model`), plus 2D Chamfer and Thread (`top_z`). So a default operation in a document with a vise is wrong at generate.

Cause (v0.19.0): `operation/heights.rs` resolves both references through `setup_align::solid_aabb_in` -> `model::solid_world_aabb`, which walks `model::model_entities`. `model::is_model` leaves out stock, WCS, tools, operations, setups and program entries, but **not fixtures**. The fixture's setup is not considered either.

## Reproduction (headless, `camcraft-cli mcp`)

A plain 50 x 50 x 6 mm block (STL), moved to Z 4..10. Box stock 55 x 55 x 11 (Z 0..11). WCS at the stock top centre. Tool `EM-0600-4FL`. One `2D Contour` with its defaults (top = Top of Model, bottom = Bottom of Model).

```
import_model {path: block.stl, name: block}
move_model   {name: block, position: [-25, -25, 4]}
set_stock    {box: {dx: 55, dy: 55, dz: 11}}
set_wcs      {stock_point: {x: center, y: center, z: max}}
add_builtin_vise {size: "5 in", position: [0, 27.5, -36.1], opening: 55}   # jaw tops at Z 2, below the part
add_tool     {catalog: EM-0600-4FL}
add_operation {kind: "2D Contour", tool: EM-0600-4FL, name: Op, source: block}
generate; verify; post {output: out.nc, post: Fanuc}
```

| | Bottom of Model resolves to | Top of Model resolves to | Generate | Verify / post |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| No vise | Z 4 (part bottom), posted Z-7.0 | Z 10 | ok | ok, posts levels Z-1 / -6 / -7 |
| Vise below the part (jaw tops Z 2) | **Z -99.6, the vise base** (WCS Z -110.6) | Z 10 | **ok, no warning** | **blocked**: `flute at move 32 strikes a fixture`, `shank at move N strikes a fixture`, `rapid at move N strikes a fixture`, plus `shank/holder ... collides with the part or an island` (722 findings) |
| Vise fitted to the stock (`fit_to_stock: true`, jaw tops Z 38.1) | Z -63.5 | **Z 38.1, the jaw tops** | refused: `Contour: nothing to machine: no material at z = 38.100 - the source spans Z4.000 to Z10.000` | - |
| Vise declared in another setup (`add_setup Setup 2`, vise `setup: Setup 2`), op in the first setup | still the vise base | - | ok | blocked as above |

To confirm the depth, the op was generated with the vise, then the vise was untagged (`remove_fixture`; the op stays `ok`, the model stays) and posted. The post was then refused with `gouge: program cuts below the model in 3920 cell(s), worst 63.50 mm at (-27.31, -27.31, z -99.60)`. The generated path goes to the vise base, Z -99.6.

## Severity

- **The post blocks it** in every case I tried: the fixture collision check catches the flute in the vise. So no gouging G-code was written.
- **It is still wrong output at generate.** Generate reports `ok` with no warning for a path that goes 100 mm into the vise. The only signal is hundreds of verify findings that read as a collision, not "your heights point at the vise".
- In the user's project the workaround was to measure **every** height from Top of Stock.
- The safety still depends on the fixture check catching every case. A fixture tagged in another setup still moves this setup's heights (last row), and the depth comes from steel the op never sees as material.

## Expected

`Top of Model` / `Bottom of Model` are the **part(s)**: the models the op machines (or the setup's non-fixture models). They never include fixtures, accessories, plates, vises, or a stock-source model. A fixture placed in setup B never changes setup A's heights.

**Done means:** with a built-in vise (and an imported fixture) placed, a default 2D Contour on a part resolves Bottom of Model to the part bottom and Top of Model to the part top, in the setup that holds the fixture and in any other setup. A pinning test generates a contour with and without a vise and asserts identical Z levels. The same holds for every kind whose heights default to the model references.

Related: #339 (fixtures/vises), #1094 (a stock-source model judged as a part - the same "which models are the part" question).

body:
Asked for by the user (2026-11-13, in chat): research-only issue for waterjet support, starting from the WAZER desktop waterjet the user owns. **Research, not code.** Pick never takes this issue; it is answered in comments and broken into sub-issues.

## Sources and clean-room rules

Clean-room rules for this research:
- **Used:** WAZER's public documentation (its support article on G-code and its materials and specs page; URLs below, cited, not copied), the Pro WAZER user manual (behaviour only), general abrasive-waterjet knowledge, and a behavioural analysis of the user's own job files exported by WAZER's web app (WAM). Those are about 120 programs from WAM 1.6 to 2.4, all Pro WAZER. Only their word and code usage and statistics were studied; no file is shared or committed.
- **Not used, and never to be used:** any Autodesk Fusion or HSMWorks post or output for WAZER (one exists in Autodesk's post library; it was not opened), WAM's JavaScript, and the machine's firmware.
- **Licence:** WAZER's G-code page is proprietary ("all rights reserved"). It is a published description of the dialect, not an open specification. Facts such as code numbers and meanings may be implemented; its text may not be copied.

## Findings so far

**Dialect** (WAM output, meanings as WAZER publishes them):
- **Modes:** G21 (mm) and G90 only. Moves are G0 and G1 only: **no arcs**, so curves are short segments. **No Z axis.** F is in mm/min. Dwell is `G4 S<seconds>`.
- **Jet and abrasive:** M3/M5 open and close the water, M8/M9 the abrasive.
- **Machine-specific M codes:** start and end of job (no M2/M30), the cut's bounding box (used by the machine's "check cut extents"), re-pierce time after a pause, and header metadata (WAM version, material name truncated to 20 characters, thickness, estimated time).
- **File format:** CRLF line endings, `;` comments, a fixed parameter header.
- **Origin:** top-left of the bed, Y negative toward the front. The cutting area is about 460 × 305 mm.
- **Per contour:** rapid to the pierce point, water on, abrasive on, stationary pierce dwell, straight lead-in, contour, then a short dwell, abrasive off, dwell, water off, dwell. The jet is never on during a rapid.
- **Kerf:** compensation is in the geometry (about half the published kerf), with no G41/G42.
- **Tabs** are uncut gaps (most contours are open).
- **Cut order:** inner contours first.
- **Feed:** the file's top F is the material rate for the chosen quality. The three qualities run at about 1 : 1.14 : 1.29. **Corner slowdown is written into F** in steps, down to about 0.45×.

**Machine:** kerf about 1.1 mm (0.044 in), maximum about 75 ipm; the pressure differs between the Pro and desktop models. The manual's error list includes a refusal of files generated by a much older WAM than the firmware.

**Materials and speeds:** the public page gives, per material and thickness, a cut rate and pierce time for each of the Pro and desktop machines. The published Pro rates sit near WAM's fine-to-medium rates; WAM's pierce times are often shorter than the published ones.

**Warranty and terms:** WAZER states that only WAM-generated files are approved, and that **edited or third-party-generated files void the warranty and breach its terms of service.** A community report says non-WAM files can leave uncut sections after pause and resume. Any CamCraft WAZER post must carry this warning prominently and must not claim WAZER approval.

## Open questions (answer before any sub-issue)

1. **Should CamCraft ship a WAZER post at all,** given the warranty and terms-of-service statement, or only a generic abrasive-waterjet post plus a user-supplied machine file? Decide with the maintainer.
2. **Pause and resume:** what does the firmware need for a third-party program to resume correctly (re-pierce after a pause, the bounding-box words)? Can that be learned from public docs alone?
3. **The corner-slowdown model:** derive it from public waterjet literature (taper and lag versus speed) rather than copying WAM's step table. What do the references say?
4. **Pierce data:** reuse #1521 (pierce and dwell data keyed by material and thickness), with waterjet as a process kind there?
5. **The operation:** a 2D abrasive-waterjet profile op, or a waterjet mode of the existing plasma/laser profile? Covers kerf offset in the geometry, leads on open contours, tabs as gaps, inner contours first, and arc linearisation tolerance.
6. **The machine file:** bed envelope and origin, kerf, max feed, model-specific speed tables (Pro vs desktop) and the bounding-box limit check.
7. **WAM project files (`.wzr`):** these are JSON with the source drawing and settings, undocumented. Importing them is out of scope unless WAZER documents the format; record that decision.

## Candidate sub-issues (filed only after the questions above are answered)

- Abrasive-waterjet profile operation (kerf, leads, tabs as gaps, inner-first order)
- Waterjet corner-slowdown and pierce-time model from published literature
- WAZER (Pro and desktop) machine definition and post, from the public dialect, with the warranty warning
- Waterjet process data in #1521's pierce and dwell tables

## Public references

- WAZER, "Understanding G-code": https://support.wazer.com/resources/preprocessing-temp/understanding-g-code
- WAZER materials and specs: https://wazer.com/materials/materials-specs/
- WAZER web app (WAM): https://wam.wazer.com/wazercam (a JavaScript app; no format docs without logging in)

Related: #1521 (plasma, laser and waterjet pierce and dwell data).

Done means: each open question is answered in a comment, the sub-issues are filed (one `P*`, one `effort:*`, `area:*`, `source:agent`, a Done means line and "Part of #<this>"), and this umbrella is closed with links to them.

body:
Found while fixing #1504 (PR #1522), beside #1503 (PR #1513).

What happens: two laws now confine an endpoint-and-width slot to its picks.
- `machining2d::slot_room::SlotBound` (PR #1522, plain Slot) reads two opposite straight edges or one face/ring. It seeds the fit and refuses, with numbers, a slot too wide, too long or past the picks.
- `operation::slot_fit::refuse_unfit_slot` (PR #1513, Trochoidal slot) is a capsule-in-region law over the picked region. Its region comes from `selection_region`, which refuses open edge runs, so a Trochoidal slot picked by two edges is refused before the law runs.

Expected: one law that both kinds call. Two ways to get there: the Trochoidal slot reads its picks through `operation::slot_bound_of` and calls `SlotBound::confine`, or `refuse_unfit_slot` becomes a thin wrapper over it. Then both kinds accept edge picks, refuse with the same messages and use one tolerance (`FIT_TOL` 0.01 mm on one side, 1e-4 mm on the other).

Done means: one confine function called by both slot arms; a Trochoidal slot picked by two opposite edges is fitted or refused by name exactly like a Slot; the pins of #1504 and #1503 still pass.

title: Plasma, laser and waterjet tools: pierce and dwell data (multi-stage pierce, heights, gas, head motion) keyed by material and thickness

body:
> bug; tools like plasma cutter - or laser for that matter, and prob waterjet as well. Would require piercing and dwell data.. Lasers usually have 1-4 piercing steps that can be used all or just one. just to get thru different thickness of material. Same with plasma.. piercing height, power at height, pressure of gas, movement of torch/laser head etc etc. Use perplexit to research this in a subagent and make a issue ticket from it where this types of tools getter better coverage.

(Maintainer, 2026-11-13, in chat.)

## What exists today

- Plasma only. `ToolKind::Torch` (`crates/tools/src/tools.rs`) is a kerf width plus rpm 0; it carries no cutting data. I found no laser or waterjet tool kind in `tools.rs`.
- The plasma operation (`crates/motion/src/plasma/mod.rs`, `emit.rs`; app side `crates/app/src/operation/types/plasma.rs`, `crates/app/src/project/plasma_dto.rs`; page `crates/ui/src/egui_app/plasma_page.rs`) has three optional per-operation numbers: pierce height, cut height, pierce delay. Left empty means "set by the controller" (AutoFS).
- The Tormach plasma post (`assets/posts/tormach-plasma.cps`) writes M207/M208/M209 for those three values and G16 for the pierce, and leaves volts, amps and gas to the control's own table. Nothing else (power, gas, pressure, torch motion at the pierce) can be stated anywhere.
- Related open issues: 621 (plasma research umbrella), 1447 (common-line cutting and marking), 1452 (DXF import for 2D cuts). No open issue covers pierce data; a "pierce" search finds only closed plasma work (670, 671).

## What is missing

1. Cut data lives on the operation, not on the tool, and is not keyed by material or thickness. Changing plate thickness means re-typing numbers.
2. Only one pierce, with one height and one delay. No transfer height, no puddle-jump (lift after pierce), no creep or start-speed ramp on exit, no amperage or gas on the tool.
3. Laser and waterjet have no tool kind, so there is nowhere to put multi-stage pierce data.
4. Posts have no way to say "this stage cannot be written in this dialect".

## Research summary (facts and concepts only, own words)

Plasma
- Transfer height: the low height where the arc first transfers to the plate. Pierce height: the higher height held while the arc pierces (limits spray onto the torch). Pierce delay: time held after transfer before the head moves. Cut height: stand-off while cutting. Torch height control holds a target arc voltage as a stand-in for the distance during the cut.
- Puddle jump (optional): after the pierce, lift to a percentage of pierce height for a short dwell to clear molten metal, then drop to cut height.
- Each system and consumable set has a maximum pierce thickness; thicker plate needs an edge start (the arc begins off the plate edge). Kerf comes from the cut chart.
- The maker's cut chart is the source of values (current, gas type and pressure, heights, voltage, speed). It normally sits in the control's material table; the program selects it and may override single values.

Laser
- Makers document up to four sequential pierce stages, each with its own time, power, pulse frequency, duty cycle, focus, nozzle distance, gas type and pressure; a stage with zero time is skipped. Parameters may ramp from a start to an end value inside a stage.
- Pierce kinds named by makers: ramped, pulsed (gradual), and a forceful short pierce; definitions vary by machine, so the data model must not hard-code them.
- Cooling dwell or gas blow is machine-specific; no standard length exists.
- Normal practice: the technology table (material and thickness) holds the recipe, the NC program selects the table and pierce type and may override.

Waterjet
- Methods: stationary, dynamic (moving toward the path while piercing), wiggle or circular (short oscillation), and low-pressure or pressure-ramp pierce for brittle or laminated material (glass, stone, ceramic, composites). Abrasive can be delayed after water starts, or fed first with pressure ramped up from low.
- No universal pierce time by thickness exists; it depends on material, pressure, nozzle and method, so it must be the user's value.

Control table versus program: recipes are usually in the control's table (selected by material and thickness) with the program choosing and sometimes overriding. A CAM system therefore needs both: store the recipe, then either post the selector or post explicit values, by dialect.

## Proposed data model

A cut-data record per tool, keyed by material and thickness (rows the user adds, copies and deletes):

- Cut parameters: cut height, feed, kerf; for plasma amperage, gas type and pressure, arc voltage; for laser power, frequency, duty, gas type and pressure, nozzle distance, focus; for waterjet pressure and abrasive flow.
- Pierce: an ordered list of 0 to 4 stages, every stage optional and individually enableable. Each stage has height, duration (dwell), power or pressure, frequency and duty (laser), gas and pressure, an optional ramp end value, and head motion during the pierce (none, wiggle or circular amplitude, or moving toward the path). Plasma uses one stage plus optional transfer height and puddle-jump (percent and dwell). Waterjet adds method, low-pressure value and abrasive delay.
- Pierce capacity per record: maximum pierceable thickness, and whether an edge start is allowed.
- Every number is entered by the user or copied from the maker's chart. Shipped example rows are marked "example" in the file and in the UI.

Editing: a cut-data table on the tool page (undoable commands, an MCP tool and script verb per the command law). The operation chooses a row (or "none: the machine's own table") and may override single values; overrides are commands too.

Operation behaviour: pierce at the start of the lead-in, run the stages in order (height move, dwell and head motion per stage), then the cut-height move and lead-in. The generated path carries the stages as records in the CL file so the post and the verifier read the same data.

Posts: each dialect writes the stages it can (dwell, height moves, selector codes or direct values). A stage or value the dialect cannot express makes the post refuse with a named reason, or write a visible comment line naming what was left to the control; it is never dropped silently. The Tormach post keeps M207/M208/M209 for the plasma values and refuses a multi-stage laser record.

## Safety rules

- A thickness above the tool's pierce capacity is refused, unless the operation states an edge start (then the lead-in must start off the plate, and that is verified).
- No silent default for a pierce time or height: an empty value either posts "controller's table" as an explicit, commented choice on a dialect that has one, or refuses.
- Stage values are checked at command creation (non-negative times and heights, power within 0 to 100 percent, at most four stages).
- Values are the user's and the machine maker's; shipped examples are labelled as examples and nothing was run on a real machine. Verification (stage order, pierce inside a kept part, head motion hitting a neighbour) joins the existing plasma laws.
- This changes posted output, so it is at least effort:high.

## Suggested slices

1. Tool-side cut-data record for the existing plasma torch (material and thickness rows, transfer height, puddle jump, pierce capacity), project file round-trip, undoable commands, MCP tool. The operation picks a row.
2. Plasma generation and the Tormach post use the row; refusal for thickness above capacity and the edge-start rule; laws and goldens.
3. Laser tool kind and machine kind with 1 to 4 pierce stages; CL records and a first laser post (dwell and height moves, explicit comment lines).
4. Waterjet tool kind: pierce methods, low-pressure pierce, abrasive delay; post support.
5. Docs and shipped example rows.

Slices 3 and 4 may need their own research issues for machine kinds; file them when slice 1 lands.

Done means: a plasma, laser or waterjet tool carries material and thickness keyed cut data with up to four ordered optional pierce stages; the operation uses the chosen row at the lead-in start; each post writes every stage or refuses or comments what it cannot; a too-thick plate without an edge start is refused; tests pin all of these.

Related: 621, 1447, 1452, 670, 671.

## Sources

- https://linuxcnc.org/docs/master/html/en/plasma/qtplasmac.html
- https://linuxcnc.org/docs/html/plasma/plasma-cnc-primer.html
- https://xnet.hypertherm.com/Xnet/library/download/?file=HYP104561
- https://www.hypertherm.com/resources/more-resources/articles/thick-metal-cutting-techniques/
- https://www.hypertherm.com/resources/more-resources/articles/torch-height-control-for-plasma-cutting/
- https://studylib.net/doc/25809509/amada-cnc-laser-machine-program-manual--2-
- https://www.fanuc.co.jp/en/product/catalog/pdf/cnc/FS30i-LB_0i-LFPlus(E)-03.pdf
- http://www.apasi.net/system/files/9999/2014/P338EN.pdf
- https://pdfcoffee.com/1-user-manual-hd-f-hd-fl-pdf-free.html
- https://www.omax.com/news/blog/4-piercing-methods-abrasive-waterjet-machining
- https://www.aquajet.co.uk/4-piercing-methods/
- https://digitallibrarynasampe.org/data/pdfs/s2019_pdfs/TP19--1458.pdf
- https://patents.google.com/patent/US9108297B2/en

body:
Reported by the maintainer (2026-11-13, in chat): "you can accidentaly deselect an operations face even when you are on a different tab and working. There is no real "selection" mode that then is locked while you work on the rest of the settings."

What happens: while an operation's dialog is open, a click in the viewport adds or removes geometry from the operation's selection whichever tab is showing (Tool, Heights, Passes, ...). A click meant to orbit, inspect or just focus the viewport silently drops a picked face, and the operation then generates on different geometry.

Expected: picking is a mode. Viewport clicks change the operation's geometry only while the Geometry tab's pick is active (the tab is showing, or its pick row is armed). On every other tab the selection is locked: clicks do not change it, the picked geometry stays highlighted, and the dialog shows plainly whether picking is on or off.

Rules:
- A selection change stays an undoable command (Ctrl+Z restores a face removed by mistake); the lock is ephemeral UI state, not a command.
- With the lock on, a viewport click does nothing to the operation's geometry; it does not fall through to a model or operation selection change that closes or swaps the dialog either.
- Same behaviour for every operation dialog and every pick row (faces, edges, points, entry positions).

Related: issue 1505 (faint edge highlight, sporadic Ctrl/Shift picking) and issue 1507 (hover highlights the selection a row would delete) touch the same pick code.

Done means: a ui harness test opens an operation with a picked face, switches to another tab, clicks the face in the viewport and asserts the selection is unchanged; on the Geometry tab the same click toggles it and undo restores it; the structural test covers the "picking on/off" indication.

body:
Asked for by the user (2026-11-13, in chat): "create a new issue for 'stock' soft jaws, so they can just be selected in CamCraft? We could just ask the user for dimensions, too."

## Today

The built-in **Soft jaw** workholding accessory (#789, `crates/app/src/accessory.rs`) is a plain block, `SoftJaw { width, height, thickness }`, defaulting to 6 × 2 × 0.75 in. The user types every size, and there are no bolt holes and no nest.

## What

1. **Stock soft-jaw presets** in the accessory picker (GUI, MCP and script), grouped by vise size, plus **Custom…** that asks for the dimensions. Sizes are the common machinable-blank sizes sold for Kurt-type vises: length × height × thickness, bolt-hole centres, screw size. Published catalog values (one vendor's public listings, 2026-11-13; generic sizes, no vendor names in the product):

   | Vise | L × H × T (in) | Bolt centres (in) | Screw |
   |---|---|---|---|
   | 4" | 4 × 2 × 1 | 2.500 | 3/8 |
   | 4" | 4 × 1.5 × 1 | – | – |
   | 5" | 5.2 × 2 × 1 | 3.125 | 3/8 or M10 |
   | 6" | 6 × 2 × 0.75 | 3.875 | 1/2 or M12 |
   | 6" | 6 × 2 × 1 | 3.875 | 1/2 or M12 |
   | 6" | 6 × 2 × 1.5 | 3.875 | 1/2 or M12 |
   | 6" | 6 × 2.5 × 1 | 3.875 | 1/2 or M12 |
   | 8" | 8 × 3 × 1 | 4.750 | 5/8 |
   | 8" | 8 × 3 × 1.5 | 4.750 | 5/8 |

   A dash means not published; hole height from the bottom and the counterbore size are not published for any size. Presets are a convenience list in a data file the user can extend, not a vendor catalog. Units follow the document. Material is a choice (aluminum or steel), for the sim and for feeds.

2. **Bolt holes in the jaw model:** two counterbored holes at the stated centres. Their height and counterbore are user-editable, with a stated default and a visible "assumed, measure your jaw" note. Then a toolpath that machines into the jaw (next point) is collision-checked against the screws.

3. **A nest from the part ("machine the part into the jaws"):** for a second setup, the jaw pair gets a pocket shaped like the part's outline at the grip height, plus a clearance offset, as an operation or a fixture feature. This gives:
   - one project that **cuts the soft jaws** (the jaws are the stock) with an ordinary 2D pocket, refusing corners tighter than the tool radius;
   - a **later setup** that uses the same jaws, with the nest, as its fixture, so the collision check sees the real pocket and not a plain block.

   Today this takes an external CAD model of the nested jaw imported as a model fixture.

## Done means

- The accessory picker offers the presets above by vise size, and Custom asks for L × H × T, bolt centres and screw. Presets load from a data file in `assets/`.
- The jaw model carries its bolt holes and counterbores. A pin shows a nest pocket that would cut into a counterbore being refused by name.
- A soft-jaw nest can be generated from a part's outline (clearance offset, grip depth) and used both as the stock of a jaw-cutting setup and as the fixture of a later setup. A pin shows the later setup's collision check seeing the pocket.
- Each change is an undoable command, with its MCP tool and a structural UI test.

Related: #789 (soft jaw accessory), #339 (fixtures/vises), #1262 (workholding docs, second setups).

The Sodick wire post of issue 617 (`assets/posts/sodick-wire.cps`) refuses a 4-axis Wire Contour by name ("is a 4-axis cut - ... no G74 / G75 or U V words").

Wanted: the 4-axis cut (upper and lower profile, PARAM WireFourAxis, WireU / WireV) in Sodick's own words. body:
Part of #1446 (first slice: the motion-crate generator, `camcraft_motion::machining2d::rest_plan` / `rest_pocket`, on branch `issue/1446-rest-2d`).

Asked for by the maintainer (2026-11-13, quoted on #1446): "We wanna cover some of the toolpaths and things like that at first." and "Lets create issues on your suggestions, they made sense." Sources as he asked: "We should use perplexity to find literature on those types of toolpaths and not copy them straight up".

What the first slice leaves out of the generator, each of which needs design before code:

1. **2D Adaptive over a rest area.** `rest_pocket` refuses the Adaptive strategy by name. The adaptive plan picks its own entry and bounds engagement assuming a full pocket; over a rest area the entry should stand in cleared floor and the engagement model must know what is already cut.
2. **Entry from already-cut space.** The first slice plunges into each rest area like a plain pocket, so nothing depends on the cleared-area estimate. Entering sideways from cleared floor is faster, and makes that estimate safety-critical: the cleared area must be read small (it is today) and the entry refused, by name, where it cannot be proved.
3. **The previous tool from the previous operations.** Today the previous tool is entered by hand and trusted (the path says so in a note). The issue also asks for "from previous operations": the cleared area measured from the stock the earlier operations of the setup leave, including their depth - a rest pass must not assume a depth the roughing never reached. Where the carried stock cannot be established, refuse by name or mark incomplete; never guess.
4. **Zigzag.** Refused by name in the first slice because rows leave cusps along the walls of a rest area. A row plan with a closing ring per rest area would lift the refusal.

Literature to start from (cited in the first slice): Held, "On the Computational Geometry of Pocket Machining", LNCS 500, 1991; Veeramani and Gau, Computer-Aided Design 29(12), 1997, and IIE Transactions 32, 2000; Yao, Gupta and Nau, Computer-Aided Design 35(9), 2003. No code or text from any other CAM product (Clean-Room Protocol).

Done means: each of the four is either built with its pinning tests (verifier clean, no rapid into material the cleared-area reading cannot prove cut, refusals named) or split into its own issue with a recorded decision; the literature used is cited in the PR.

body:
Asked for by the user (2026-11-13, in chat): "Can we setup a build test post merge using local gh runner?"

## Why

AGENTS.md "Fixes are tested in the background" has the main session dispatch a gate-runner agent to run the batch tier on `origin/main` after a fix merges, in the shared main checkout. That costs agent tokens. It blocks the main checkout and any cut meanwhile. It's skipped when a session is busy, so several PRs that were each tested alone merge untested together: today #1432, #1165 and #1181 merged in one batch, after #1405, #1397, #1421 and #1436. The self-hosted Linux runner from #1413 / PR #1418 can run this for free.

## What

A workflow, e.g. `.github/workflows/post-merge.yml`:
- **Trigger:** `push` to `main` only, plus `workflow_dispatch` (input: ref). This is the "user's say-so" AGENTS.md requires for a `push` trigger. Only merged, reviewed code reaches `main`, so no fork can run code on the runner. Never `pull_request` or `pull_request_target`.
- **Runner:** `runs-on: [self-hosted, linux]` (0 billed minutes).
- **Concurrency:** one group for `main` with `cancel-in-progress: true`, so a burst of merges tests only the newest head. The runner is also the cut runner; a cut must not be starved, so say how they share it (e.g. the cut's jobs take priority, or post-merge yields while a `release/*` cut is running).
- **Gate:** `cargo xtask gate batch` (no release-mode heavy lanes; target ≤ 20 min), wrapped in `xvfb-run -a` for the UI suites. Always upload `gate-logs/` as an artifact.
- **On red:** the run fails visibly. Decide how agents and the maintainer hear about it: e.g. the job comments on, or opens, one rolling `main is red` issue (P1, or P0 when it's a G-code test) naming the failing suites and the commit range, and closes it on the next green run. Keep it to one issue, not one per run.
- **Permissions:** `contents: read`, and `issues: write` only on the reporting step.

## Also changes

AGENTS.md "Fixes are tested in the background" (the workflow replaces the gate-runner dispatch; the local batch stays the fallback when the runner is down), and "GitHub Actions minutes are budgeted" (a `push` trigger on `main` to the self-hosted runner only). It's a process change, so it bumps `.claude/PROCESS_VERSION` and gets announced on #681. A `.github` change gets `needs-maintainer`.

Builds on #1413 (PR #1418, the self-hosted runner and its AGENTS.md section): stack on it, or wait for it to merge.

Done means: a merge to `main` starts the batch gate on the self-hosted runner without anyone dispatching it; a red run tells the agents (the rolling issue); a green run closes that issue; bursts of merges test only the newest head; a cut is never blocked by it; and AGENTS.md says so.
